Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

issues.explanation: For a witnessed-other-trauma profile, 'being seen' and 'being criticised or corrected' are hard to reconcile as primary trauma triggers unless the witnessed event specifically involved scrutiny or humiliation; nothing else in the profile supports that context.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected
issues.explanation: The formulation has a strong Triggers → Threat link, so trigger content should plausibly map onto the endorsed threat meanings. 'Time of day the event occurred' links well with hypervigilance to sounds, but 'being seen' and 'being criticised' do not connect clearly to the selected threat items.

vignette: Amir's eyes darted back and forth, scanning the crowded fast food restaurant where he worked. It was a typical Friday evening rush, but for Amir, it felt like a minefield waiting to explode. Every loud clang of pots or pans in the kitchen made him jump, transporting him back to that fateful day three years ago. Amir had been working as a cook at a busy street food stall in his hometown when a rival vendor's argument escalated into a violent brawl. Amir watched in horror as one man was severely beaten, the sounds of breaking glass and crunching metal still echoing in his mind. The police arrived just as the attacker fled, but not before yelling a chilling threat to the victim. The trauma of that day lingered, manifesting in unexpected ways. Amir became increasingly sensitive to criticism or correction from his managers or coworkers. A careless remark about his cooking technique would send him into a tailspin, convinced he was on the verge of being fired or worse. His colleagues began to notice his defensiveness and avoidance of feedback, but Amir couldn't shake the feeling that one misstep would lead to catastrophe. As time passed, Amir's world shrunk to a tiny, manageable sphere. He only felt safe in a handful of places: his small apartment, the restaurant during off-peak hours, or walking alone in quiet neighborhoods at dawn. Any deviation from this routine made him anxious, as if he was tempting fate. His sleep began to suffer, with nightmares about missed orders and botched meals jolting him awake. The same time of day the event occurred – late afternoon on Fridays – became a trigger for Amir's heightened alertness. He'd find himself scanning the restaurant for potential threats, his heart racing in anticipation of some unknown disaster. Loud noises only added to his distress, as if the cacophony might mask an incoming attack. Amir began to dread delays or unexpected setbacks, convinced that something terrible was lurking just beneath the surface. A slow-moving customer would prompt him to wonder if someone had been injured outside; a brief power outage would send him searching for signs of sabotage. His coworkers grew concerned about his increasing paranoia and irritability, but Amir couldn't explain why he felt this way – only that it made sense to be vigilant. One particularly grueling shift ended with Amir's manager suggesting he take a few days off to recharge. The criticism stung, but what finally brought him to seek help was the realization that his hyper-vigilance had begun to seep into his dreams, even infecting his quiet moments of solitude. He longed for a sense of safety and calm, but feared that acknowledging his vulnerabilities would only invite disaster. As Amir sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with his hands, he whispered a confession: "I just want to be able to work without feeling like I'm walking on eggshells all day. I don't know how much more of this I can take."
